entities.summary: Slánoll, son of Ollom Fotla, was, according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition, a High King of Ireland. He succeeded to the throne on the death of his brother Fínnachta. It is said that there was no disease during his reign. After a reign of fifteen, seventeen, or thirty years, he was found dead of unknown causes in his bed in Tara and was succeeded by his brother Géde Ollgothach. When his body was dug up forty years later by his son Ailill, it showed no sign of decomposition. The chronology of Geoffrey Keating's Foras Feasa ar Éirinn dates his reign to 895–880 BC, while the Annals of the Four Masters places it between 1257 and 1241 BC.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Slánoll's reign is notable for being one of the longest in Irish historical records, spanning between 895–880 BC according to Geoffrey Keating's Foras Feasa ar Éirinn. His unusual longevity and lack of disease during his rule make him a subject of interest in medieval Irish legend.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Slánoll's reign is notable for being the longest without disease in recorded history, with some estimates suggesting a period of 15-30 years. This unusual circumstance has led to speculation about the environmental and social conditions during his time.
